extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators (trial attorneys), and juries in patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials covering claim construction, types of infringement, and statutory/theory-specific elements the jury must find (e.g., literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents, inducement, contributory infringement, §271(f)/(g) claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent claims are numbered sentences at the end of the patent ... The claims are intended to define, in words, the boundaries of the inventor’s rights. Only the claims of the patent can be infringed. Neither the written description, nor the drawings of a patent can be infringed. Each of the claims must be considered individually. You must use the same claim meaning for both your decision on infringement and your decision on invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deciding infringement or invalidity, jurors must understand the patent claims. Claims define the scope of rights; only claims (not description/drawings) can be infringed; apply same meaning for infringement and invalidity; consider each claim separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for the Case
rubrics_metrics.description: It is my job as judge to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings I give you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge provides constructions; for claim limitations not construed, use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the alleged invention (Teva/Phillips/Markman authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The asserted claims ... include a limitation in a special form called means[[step]]-plus-function. ... This element does not cover all [[means] [steps]] that perform the recited function of “___________________________.” Rather, I have determined that the recited function is “_____________________.” I have determined that the corresponding [[structure] [step]] described in the patent specification and drawings that perform this recited function is “_______________________________,” or an equivalent of this corresponding [[structure] or [step]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give Instruction 2.2 only if the case involves means-plus-function claims. Where limitation uses 'means for' or 'step for', jury may incorrectly think limitation includes any component that accomplishes the function; instruction clarifies that only corresponding structure (and equivalents) in specification are covered (35 U.S.C. §112 ¶6/§112(f) and cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim. Patent law gives the owner of a valid patent the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling ... Any person or business entity that has engaged in any of those acts without the patent owner’s permission infringes the patent. You must compare the Defendant’s accused product/method to the claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compare accused product to plaintiff’s commercial product. Distinguish direct vs indirect infringement, literal vs doctrine of equivalents, and induced vs contributory infringement to avoid jury confusion (practice note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge and Intent Are Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: The Defendant is liable for directly infringing ... if you find that the Plaintiff has proven that it is more likely than not that Defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim of the patent during the term of the patent. A party can directly infringe a patent without knowing of the patent or without knowing that what the party is doing is patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement under 35 U.S.C. §271(a) requires making/using/etc. the claimed invention; subjective knowledge/intent is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if Defendant's product/method includes each and every element/method step recited in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. If the accused product lacks one or more recited elements/steps, there is no literal infringement. Same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement (Attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may find that the Defendant directly infringes if you find (1) that Defendant personally performed all acts necessary to infringe, or (2) that the steps performed by the other party are attributable to the Defendant. Steps are attributable if Defendant exercised direction or control over the other party or Defendant and the other party formed a joint enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: (1) agreement among group members; (2) common purpose; (3) community of pecuniary interest; (4) equal right to a voice in direction (equal right of control). If neither personal performance nor attribution is found, no direct infringement. Practice note: joint infringement and inducement are closely related—consider instructing together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement, Plaintiff must prove that (1) the part of the Defendant’s product or step performs the recited function, and (2) is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the patent specification and drawings for performing this recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First decide whether accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the specific function. If so, decide whether that structure/step is the same as, or equivalent to, the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence may be shown by insubstantial differences or by performing substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result (POSITA perspective). If function not performed or structure not the same/equivalent, no infringement of the means-plus-function limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim. A dependent claim includes all elements recited in the dependent claim, as well as all elements of the independent claim to which it refers. To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, Plaintiff must show the Defendant’s product/method includes each and every element of both the independent and dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read independent claims separately; if the independent claim is not literally infringed, then the dependent claim also is not literally infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Claim Preamble Phrases: 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative 1: 'comprising' means 'including the following but not excluding others.' Alternative 2: 'consisting of' means 'including the following and excluding others.' Alternative 3: 'consisting essentially of' means 'including the following and possibly including unlisted components that do not materially affect the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim preamble uses 'comprising', accused product that includes all claimed elements literally infringes even with additional components. If 'consisting of', additional components negate literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of', literal infringement exists if additional components do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Defendant’s product/method does not literally infringe an asserted claim, you must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by including components/method steps that are equivalent to those elements not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine each missing element individually to see if the accused product has an equivalent. Equivalence may be shown by (a) only insubstantial differences from the claimed element, or (b) performing substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Consider whether, at the time of alleged infringement, a person of ordinary skill would have known of interchangeability; known interchangeability is not necessary. If claim is literally infringed, no need to apply DOE. Practice notes and case law govern limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on DOE—Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Court has determined that prosecution history estoppel applies, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to certain elements of the asserted claims that were surrendered by the patentee through representation or a narrowing amendment for reasons related to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction should be given only if the Court determines estoppel applies as a matter of law. The Court will list elements to which DOE cannot be applied; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Cited cases: Festo, Warner-Jenkinson, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on DOE—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Court determines that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to the listed elements of the asserted claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction is given only if the Court determines dedication applies as a matter of law. The Court will list elements; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Cited cases: SanDisk, Pfizer v. Teva, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement) — Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that Defendant actively induced infringement, Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (A) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps), and (B) Defendant actively induced these acts of infringement by the alleged direct infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove active inducement, Plaintiff must establish it is more likely than not that: (1) Defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with the intent to cause acts by alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) Defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness; (3) Defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one patent claim. Willful blindness requires subjective belief of high probability that a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by supplying (or causing to be supplied) all or a substantial portion of the components of the patented product from the United States to another country and actively inducing the assembly of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) Defendant supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) Defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into an infringing product. A 'substantial portion' is a quantitative (not qualitative) assessment; exporting a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability. Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement (§271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish contributory infringement, Plaintiff must prove that it is more likely than not that: (1) someone other than Defendant has directly infringed a claim of the patent; (2) Defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness; (3) Defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; (4) Defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (5) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (6) the component constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (7) Defendant knew that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' has non-infringing uses that are not occasional/farfetched/impractical/experimental. Defendant's knowledge that component was especially made/adapted may be shown by willful blindness (subjective high probability + deliberate actions to avoid learning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted (§271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by supplying (or causing to be supplied) a component(s) of a claimed invention from the United States into a foreign country, where the exported components were especially made or adapted for use in an invention covered by the patent and have no substantial non-infringing uses, and where Defendant knew the components were especially made or adapted and intended for the components to be combined in a way that would have infringed if combined in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show §271(f)(2) infringement, Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that: (1) Defendant actually supplied the components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) Defendant knew or should have known components were especially made/adapted for use in an infringing product; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) Defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product. In §271(f)(2) context, a 'substantial use' is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Import/Sale/Offer/Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by importing, selling, offering for sale, or using a product that was made by a process covered by one or more claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show infringement under §271(g), Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that: (1) Defendant imported into the U.S. or, within the U.S., sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between the issue date of the patent and its expiration/date of trial; and (3) [further statutory elements as applicable].
